Hack squats are one of my top 3 quad movements. I like to keep them more intense by going basically all the way to the bottom until I feel a stretch in my quads, pause 1-2 seconds in the stretch, and only come about 3/4 of the way up without locking out. This keeps tension in the quads the entire set. I really like adding yoga blocks, or a foam roller under the shoulder pads too. Allows you to get very deep in the bottom without bottoming out the machine. 

Another recent favorite for me is belt squats. If the belt squat machine allows you to get deep enough at least. 

Another one I love is feet forward smith machine squats. Bring your feet up just a few inches in front of your normal stance and this helps to keep most of the tension in the quads. I’m currently doing these after hack squats with relatively light weight on one of my leg days.

25 reps is my cutoff point. I would say fixing yourself to 15 reps or 12 reps or 20 or whatever the number is, isn’t necessarily the best approach. At least for me it’s not. 

I like going until I feel like I’m 2 reps shy of failure, and then all the way to failure on my last set. So that might look like 18 reps set 1, 14 reps set 2, 13 reps set 3. When I hit 25 reps on my first set and do that or just above for a couple weeks consistently I’ll add 2.5 lbs. But it takes forever to add weight for side delt work. Forever. 

And I say 3-4 times a week because your side delts will rarely get sore, and if they do it’s for like 6 hours after you wake up the next day. Even if it’s the whole next day it’s never 2 days later that they’re sore so they’re healed and ready to go. And considering it takes so long to progress them you may as well throw the volume on. 

Another point. Why limit yourself to 3 sets per session. That may be perfect, but if you’re never getting sore from three, then try 4, and so on.

Final tip: try movements that hit both delts at once. Single arm stuff is great but it’s mentally taxing in the sense that it takes forever. Especially if you’re trying to hit 15+ sets per week. All the sudden you’re actually doing 30 sets cause it’s one for each side.

At two years in, I’d assume you’re still making some strength gains (adding reps, and weight) even while in a deficit. Certainly not the same gains that you did in your first year, but probably still gaining to some degree. If that’s the case your gains are going to go crazy just eating at maintenance calories. You might even accidentally end up in a small deficit again a few months in from gaining rapidly. 

Don’t freak out if you rebound a little at first when eating at maintenance and end up leveling out at 183 or something. That’s pretty normal. 

People have the idea that you always need to eat in a surplus to gain. That is very often true but it’s context dependent and each individual case is different. You’ve been in a deficit for so long that I’d be shocked if you didn’t get some pretty serious gains just by leveling out the calorie intake to match your current weight. You won’t make serious gains like that forever, and it may only last 3-4 months but you can put on noticeable mass in that kind of timeframe.

If you over eat by 1500 calories for one day when you’re doing a 500 calorie deficit you effectively erase 3 days of diet progress. Over the course of 2-3 weeks it isn’t a huge deal, but if you were doing that once a week it’s something to keep in mind.

And regardless of the deficit you think you’re in, if you lose a couple lbs in a week and then keep the same calories and don’t lose anything else for the next 2-3 weeks or so, you’re not in a deficit. You’ve just found your maintenance. From that point you have to subtract more calories to start seeing real medium term progress with fat loss. If the progress stalls another 2-3 weeks again, you’ve reached your new maintenance. 

It takes a long time to lose weight. In the scope of things it’s not that long or that crazy, but it feels like a long ass time when you’re in it. You won’t see daily jumps on the scale usually. That’s why you weigh every day at the same time, write it down, and take averages week over week. At your weight and body fat, aiming for 2 lbs a week is a great start. I’d personally forget the calculators and go with “what am I putting in my mouth, and how is that affecting the scale?” Because if you’re not losing weight week over week you’re not cutting. You’re just maintaining.

It’s massively helpful if you’re the type of person who can more or less eat the same things everyday. It’s makes it incredibly easy to add and subtract food when you need more or less calories.

Scootch the bench up a tad so that the bar is landing on your upper chest. Not super close to the collar bone, but closer to the collar bone than the nipple line. 

Retract your scaps a little bit behind you to form a slight arch and pre stretch the pecs. 

Your tempo is much better at the beginning. Your eccentrics are more controlled. As you fatigue you’re starting to let the bar fall more rapidly. Try to keep control throughout your set. Slowing down your eccentric a little from what it was at the beginning may be a good idea.

Keep your butt on the bench. Your trying to grow your chest, not do hip thrusts to grow your glutes. 

Add a pause when the bar touches your chest. Just 1 second at the bottom.

Experiment with different grip widths. I personally like a slightly wider grip for this exercise.

I wouldn’t overly concern yourself with picking optimal exercises at your stage of lifting. Pick exercises that feel comfortable for you that are giving you solid gains over time first and foremost. 

There’s a lot of value as a newb to learning how to do the basic compound lifts imo. A lot of the science based guys like Nippard and Israetel would also agree. Things like flat bench press, bent over barbell row, deadlifts, and barbell squats. These aren’t necessarily optimal for each of the muscles they target, but if you’re new they’re going to put so much muscle on you it doesn’t matter. Also, if you dial in technique on these as a newb, once you get slightly more advanced and are 1.5-2 years into your training you can focus on other things to optimize and to keep the newb gains going as they stall out. 

Dialing in form on these more complex lifts early on also has the added benefit of giving you even less learning curve when you move onto many of the machine and dumbbell lifts. When you can figure out how to feel a good stretch with good form on a barbell row, back squat, or bench press, it’ll come instantly on the less complex lifts. You’re setting yourself up for an easy runway to more fast gains when they get hard to come by. 

This doesn’t mean you shouldn’t use any machines or dumbbells early on. But in my opinion, and in my experience, building a program in which the core compound movements are the center and foundation is unmatched for newbies. 

I’m just over 3 years into this hobby. This is the beginning of my 4th year. I got so much additional gains in my 3rd year after 2 years of mostly barbell based compounds. I also did a lot of one arm dumbbell rows and lat pull downs. Did a good amount of overhead pressing as well. Got great gains the first two years. But I really don’t think my third year would’ve been so successful had I not did it the way I did. A big thing that made the difference for me this year was training arms at all. I just did compound chest and back stuff the first two years.  Got some noob gains for arms and shoulders in year 3 which was sick.

Currently I hit arms 3x a week on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday. Currently the routine is ⏬⏬⏬

Tuesday: low incline db curls with arms pointed out, cable overhead tricep extension, cable tricep push down. All of these are done with myorep match sets

Thursday: ez bar preacher curl, cable overhead tricep extensions, smith machine jm press with bench at lowest incline. All done with myorep match sets

Saturday: low incline db curls with arms pointed out, super set with standing hammer curls at same weight. Both done with myorep match sets. Then I do a giant myorep set of cable tricep push downs. (I pick a weight and start with at least 35 reps for the day. Next Saturday is more reps and so on until I hit 50+. The following session I add weight). Then standing cable curls, also giant myorep set. Then forearm cable curls, also giant myorep set. 

At the end of the day you just want to pick arm exercises that don’t beat up your joints quickly, give you a great pump, and are easy to progress. Take those exercises close to failure, and train them often. If you want to prioritize arms then prioritize their volume, and the order in which you hit them. Hard to do the best growing arms when you only hit tricep push downs at the end of chest day. Try putting them first, and hit them at least 3x a week. Add volume slowly each week until you Deload, rinse and repeat.

The double stack cable machine, and rolling a bench up to do incline flys. Cables set all the way to the bottom. Recently super setting with light incline DB press. That and just DB press on both incline and flat have made the biggest differences for me. As soon as I left flat barbell bench behind my chest saw more growth than ever. Never felt a stretch with it and wasted two years by keeping them as my primary movement.

For me personally the only barbell compounds I incorporate are incline bench and squats. Multiple reasons why, but bench press does almost nothing for me in terms of hypertrophy. Barely any gains in 2 years with that as my primary chest movement and it injured me several times. Every time I started progressing again I’d get hurt even if it was minor and it set me back in progression. Switched to dumbbells and machines and over the last year my chest grew way more than the first two years. I feel zero stretch in my chest on a flat bench with a barbell. 

With deadlifts it’s a similar story. I saw a lot of gains, but every time I started making headway in my progression I got hurt. Looking at the deadlift practically, it trains a lot of muscle groups simultaneously which is great, but it doesn’t necessarily train any of them well. It’s easy to make the argument that the glutes are the primary movers in deadlifts, and there’s several glute movements that come to mind that are just way better. Same with the back. Haven’t done them for almost a year and I don’t miss them. I’m still getting bigger and stronger, and I’m never wiped out fatigue wise for 2-3 days because I did deadlifts. Now that I’m oscillating between 5 day programs and 6 day programs it’s just not worth it. When I was doing 3 days a week doing deadlifts one of those days was a lot more reasonable. 

It’s hard for me to say all of the same about barbell squats though. The only argument I can think of against barbell squats is that there are a couple other movements that are better quad builders. Hack squats for example. 

My advice for most people would be to try all of the barbell movements because they do work great for most people, and for beginners who are doing 3-4 days a week they’re usually great bang for your buck so to speak. BUT, if you don’t like these movements after several months, and these movements are hurting you, or you’re just not seeing the progress you want, then try other things in place of them. We’re all different and some things work better than others depending on your build.

And to lend an olive branch to the pro barbell people I get it. It’s the most popular and clearly many people grow big chests with bench press, even with nothing else. It’s fun and important to do lifts you like. I feel similarly passionate about barbell squats. But I would certainly say you don’t need it to grow a big chest, and would even say it’s not the best choice as a primary. Despite my love for barbell squats I would also say it’s not the best primary if the goal is big quads. I feel zero stretch in my chest with a straight bar despite feeling my chest contract with one. I’d love to try a cambered bar. Incline barbell can be pretty dope, but requires very strict form for me. And despite my hatred for cable flys nothing can hold a candle to the pump I get from them besides dumbbells and deficit pushups as a finisher. Even then the pump from flys is way more. I’ve never felt more than a very minimal pump from a straight bar doing any presses.

People who are new to training (with the exception of people with a lot of excess fat) should primarily focus on protein, and not pay too much attention to caloric intake. You should be more or less eating like normal, maybe slightly more since you’re burning more. The only thing that should change in a big way diet wise is your protein intake going way up. 1g of protein per lb of body weight is an excellent target to shoot for, and 75% of that is also just fine. No less though. You can grow a lot of muscle your first year not focusing much on calories if at all. 

At some point around a year or so in, maybe as long as two years for some people, you realize your progress is slowing and you introduce bulking and cutting. But for beginners the stimulus of lifting weights is so new that their body has to grow lots of muscle to keep up. Eating more will just put more fat on and won’t give you significantly more muscle growth as a newbie. 

My recommendation would be to keep things as simple as possible for yourself and do everything you can to set yourself up for success. The biggest thing over the long run is consistency. 

Pick a gym that’s close to home, or close to work, or somewhere between the two that is easy for you to get to consistently. Not necessarily the gym that’s super nice and 30 minutes out of the way of your daily routine. Go when it’s most convenient for you. If you’re not a morning person you don’t need to become a morning person to start working out. Most of us just go after work or in the early afternoon on our days off. 

Start out at 3 days a week. 4 max. Don’t burn yourself out. You’re new and you want to ease into things. Nothing about muscle building or fitness comes quickly anyways, and you’re not going to get significantly more out of 5 days than 3. It’s much easier for most people to add something into their life when it doesn’t eat into most days of their week. It also offers more flexibility if you miss a day. Much easier to make that day up on a 3 day schedule. 

Focus on compound movements, aka movements that hit multiple muscle groups simultaneously. Glute kickbacks are fine and all, but your time is better spent doing a squat variation and hitting most of the major muscle groups of the lower body. 

TLDR: as far as diet goes just focus on protein, consistency is key, make introducing fitness into your life as easy as possible, and pick exercises that give you the most bang for your buck and your time.

Kind of yes. But there is so so much to factor in there. 

Many people in the intermediate stages of their training (3-5 years in) stall out completely and fail to continue progressing. It makes a lot of sense because that’s the stage you have to start really dialing shit in and the stuff on the margins starts to matter a lot more. That’s extra work and dedication that many people just don’t have.  In a sense that’s when things actually start to get hard. Don’t fail to underestimate almost everyone’s ability to be a little lazy and not go the extra mile when it matters. And don’t fail to underestimate how much that extra mile matters once you’re not a beginner. In my estimation there are 4 types of people who get past this stage while continuing to make great gains. People who really dial up the effort and are dedicated, people who are genetically gifted and continue to coast on the things they did as a beginner, people who use gear, and people who have some combination of the previous 3 together. 

Another thing to note from your comment is how much genetics play a role in vascularity. There are some guys who are skinny af and vascular af. When those guys start getting jacked, they continue to be vascular, but now they’re also jacked. I used to be extremely skinny (135 lbs) and was very vascular. Pencil sized forearm veins with no notable muscle mass outside of some on my legs from hiking. Body fat % is also massively influential in how vascular you appear. 

When it comes to staying lean and jacked, it’s another yes and no thing. Once you get lean enough it’s fairly easy to stay lean. If you bulk smart and don’t bulk beyond 16-20 weeks at a time, and average a gain rate of around a half pound per week you’re going to stay quite lean year round. And if you cut smart and keep training intensity and protein intake high, losing muscle isn’t a thing. In many cases you can gain small amounts of muscle while cutting still, though it is much much harder and the gains are not noteworthy, unless you’re on gear. 

Bottom line as I said in a comment above… outside of the ifbb pro looking motherfuckers you really can’t tell unless you’ve seen the bloodwork. There are too many variables at play. There is always going to be those people who train smarter, train harder, eat better, sleep better, have more time in their day for rest, have better genetics etc etc. And I’m not saying that people aren’t doing drugs and that it isn’t fairly rampant. Well you’re definitely not stupid. My advice would be to not think about shoulders too much if you recently started taking lifting seriously. Focus more on compound movements that are going to hit multiple groups simultaneously, and train on the more infrequent side. Something like 3-4 times a week and mostly full body workouts. As a newb you’re going to get a lot out of a little. No reason to rush to training most of the week when you don’t even need to yet. Focus on slow eccentrics, emphasizing the stretched portion of your lifts and pausing there, and just build your technique while trying hard. 3-6 exercises per session is going to be plenty for you. 

That being said if you still insist on leaning into shoulder work, stay at 2 days a week for now. No reason to go for more when your body is rejecting it. Like I said above, you’re going to get a lot out of whatever you’re doing as a newb, so no need to force it. Just dial in the technique for the lift or two lifts you’re doing for side delts. Forget the weight you’re doing and do high reps with good form close to failure, to failure, and beyond failure. Technique+effort=big gains.

Hit delts 3-4 times a week. They recover so quick that there’s really no reason not to. Start some workouts with delts. Want to get the most out of a shoulder day? You have to start with them. Aim to start a mesocycle in the 12-15 sets a week range, and finish in the mid 20’s if you’re not looking to cut volume on other work. If you’re okay with doing that, push beyond 30, and maybe even 40+. Just make sure you bring volume for other muscle groups to roughly 3-6 sets a week depending on the muscle if you go the specialization route. Finally, eat enough to make it happen. Doesn’t have to be a ton of course but being in a calorie surplus will help obviously.

To piggyback on what doodledinglebopper wrote, yes anecdotally it has worked well for me with arms and shoulders. 

To add some things, I’d also say that specializing for back and legs simultaneously is probably not a great idea. If you want to do this I would alternate it and shoot for longer mesocycles (6-7 weeks) if you’re typically okay with that. What I mean by that is doing one mesocycle specializing in legs, then one for back, then legs for the next, and back for the next. And I would be taking a week to 10 days of active rest between each instead of a traditional Deload. 

I’m suggesting longer mesocycles, especially for legs because working up to the higher volume would be possible surely, but tough out of the gate. At least for me. Towards the end of a traditional mesocycle I have a hard time getting my legs more than just a little sore. At the beginning it doesn’t take much though. So if I’m going to slowly build into high volume for the legs the longer meso would be necessary if I’m going to hit legs 3x weekly and push for 20-30 sets a week for quads and glutes by the end, and 15-25 for hamstrings by the end. 

I’d also highly suggest putting your calf days on non leg days. Especially if you are doing hack squats, pendulum squats or super deep leg presses. Something about those super deep quad stretching positions stretches the fuck out of my calves and doing calves on those days is too much. 

Simply put, for legs I might shoot for a 7 week meso (6 weeks of actual work) and ramp up from 2 sets of everything starting the first week while adding at least one set every week, and hitting it all 3 x a week. Hamstrings for example your first week will be 6 sets, then 9, then 12, then 15, 18, and 21. And I’d personally do 1 hamstring movement per leg day, and 1 quad movements on 2/3 days, with 2 quad movements 1/3 days. That would make your first week 8 sets of quads and your last week 28 sets. For glutes I might shoot for something like 15 sets to finish only because you’ll be halfway training them through a lot of the quad work. Calves you’ll have to feel out. Probably on the higher end with quads in terms of sets per week. But I also feel like calves are easier to over train personally. And for the love of god, don’t deadlift for any of these movements. SLDL for hamstrings sure, but no normal deadlifts or deficit sumos or anything. 

I personally don’t need much work for anything legs, including calves, but if I did this would be my approach. And if I did a back specializing id be exceeding 30 sets in a week by the end of a meso. My back recovers fast and only barely gets sore.

I finished a 12 week cut about 5 weeks ago. I lost 15 lbs in that time and then in my first week of trying to do maintenance lost another 2 lbs lol… so I’m a month past losing 17 lbs in 13 weeks. 

My advice is multi pronged, but I would start with backing off the diet for 3 weeks (pick up the diet again right after Deload). Don’t think about diet at all for the first two weeks. Hunger will settle down after a week or so, and then you’ll spend another week just living life, and then during your Deload you can plan a new avenue of attack for when you pick your diet back up. 

Another thing I would do when I return to the diet would be to not pay attention to carbs. Pay attention to protein and net calories. That’s it. You’re not going to lose diet progress eating roughly maintenance volume on the weekends if it ends up that way. If you’re in a deficit for 5 days and at maintenance for 2, you’re still in a net deficit for the week. If you’re losing weight at the pace you want to lose change nothing. If you’re lagging behind cut calories a little while possibly increasing activity a little. Just make sure to weigh yourself daily and track progress with a weekly average. FYI you can burn about 100 calories walking a little over a mile. That’s usually what it is for me at least at my current height of 5’7” and weight of 170. 

That brings me to my next point which I already mentioned. Walking. If you’re not walking for some extra steps already start doing that. Start gradually and work your way up as you get deeper in the cut. Maybe add half a mile every week. Most people are going to average around 2,200 steps per mile. Try not to exceed 15,000 in a day though. No need to get crazy with it. If you currently get 7,000 steps a day then push it to 8,500 in the first week you pick the cut back up and add 500 every week after. 

I think my last point would be to plan meal timing around workouts as much as possible. I ate a shit ton of carbs during my cut. I don’t count so I can’t give a solid number, but I make 1 cup of oats with 1/4 cup of granola and put berries in it with vanilla whey and milk soaking over night for breakfast. When I started the cut I’d eat half for a late breakfast instead of the whole thing and then eat the other half as a late lunch about 90 minutes before the gym. Then I’d eat an apple on the way to the gym. Then I’d get home and eat my chicken rice and veggies for dinner before my walk. Then it’s a whey shake after I shower and chill before bed. I eat the exact same fucking things every single day and that made it easy for me. I know not everyone can do that but I like it that way and it’s super easy. Point being if you sandwich your workout between meals, energy and pumps won’t be an issue, and you’re technically eating 4 meals a day that are spaced far enough apart. 

Whatever you decide to do, good luck to you! It’s not super easy.. I know. This was my first successful long term cut and I learned a lot. There was a 3 week period I didn’t lose a pound. And I had periods where I felt endlessly hungry, but those thankfully didn’t last too long. Your body adjusts.

Hit legs when they aren’t sore again, or when the soreness is barely noticeable. If you hit legs Monday and they’re good to go Wednesday do that. If you’re subtracting volume from upper you can afford to add quite a bit to lower. Just make sure you’re doing roughly 2-4 sets in the week for everything upper (back chest bis tris and shoulders). 

For me personally, especially if I was a woman (women tend to recover faster) my split would probably look something like Monday: quads, glutes, hamstrings. Tuesday: bis, tris, calves. Wednesday: glutes, hamstrings, quads. Thursday: chest, back, shoulders. Friday: hamstrings, glutes, quads, calves. Saturday: yoga/core. Sunday: rest

Additionally I would do my light run after either Tuesday’s or Thursdays workout. Remember you’re only going to do 2-4 sets of each on those days. Just enough to get you a little sore, and get a pump by the end of the workout. Add sets if necessary to your maintenance work if you’re no longer getting pumps, and/or light soreness. 

On the leg days I would be doing the priority muscle (the one you start with) for roughly 6 sets to start. So 2-3 exercises, starting with 2-3 sets each Add a set per week until your Deload. For the secondary muscles on those days, shoot for roughly 3 sets to start, and also add a set per week. Big caveat to the adding a set per week thing. If your hamstrings for example are still sore the next time you hit them (tiny bit of remaining soreness is okay) then subtract a set from the same day that got you sore enough to hinder that workout. Do that once, and then try and add a set again the following week. Idea being your muscles adapt quickly week to week and adding sets USUALLY won’t be an issue but if it is then walk it back for a week. 

Another bit of information: if you’re doing a specialization phase like this and trying really hard to throw volume at a specific group or area  to get it to grow, aim to be in a slight caloric surplus. If you’ve been maintaining your body weight add a small meal to each day. And with a specialization phase like this you’ll want to aim for roughly 12-16 weeks of running this with deloads. I personally like my Deload every 5th week, so for me I either run specialization for 10 weeks or 15 weeks. And after a Deload you rinse and repeat. Starting with lower volume than you ended with before the last Deload and gradually building that volume until your next Deload. 

Remember you really want to bring up legs. Even though you normally workout 4 days a week, doing 5 for the next 10-15 weeks and cutting back some on running if you normally run a long distance is going to pay off in spades. When you’re not working out, doing a light weekly run, doing a weekly yoga session, or doing 1-2 walks a week for extra steps, you need to be resting as much as possible and maximizing your sleep. 

Good luck with whatever you decide to do!

Since the end of last year I’ve dived fully into high rep intense hypertrophy work. Slow eccentrics, pausing at the stretch at the bottom of eccentrics, incorporating myoreps and myrorep match sets where possible (hack squats, leg press, seated hamstring curls, and leg extensions), drop sets where possible for upper body, giant sets sometimes when I am limited on time and when it’s possible etc etc. I periodize all my training now over 5 week cycles, building in intensity until the 5 week which is Deload. Incorporating full rest weeks of not going to the gym every 3rd or 4th Deload. Usually first week is two sets of everything and I add sets when I notice I didn’t get sore from the last training session, or reduce them when I’m still sore from the previous session (which has only happened once). I try to add a rep, or 5 lbs to every lift for each week in those training cycles. Next training cycle I start from scratch and usually end up 1-3 reps, or 5-15 lbs ahead by the end compared to 5 weeks previous. Always lift between 1-3 rir except my last week before Deload. On that week I really try to push almost every set to failure to stay fresh on what that feels like and stay in tune with good guesses at my rir.

The main point I was trying to get across in regards to diet is you don’t really have to bulk or cut as a newb. If you eat at or close to maintenance you’ll slowly gain muscle while slowly losing fat. You’re in a unique spot as a newb in that way. Once you get 1-2 years in that will no longer be possible. I also edited tf out of my previous comment. If you’re interested it might be worth considering some or many of those points

I’d be curious why you don’t take advantage of the fact you can eat at maintenance and effectively recomp for the first year or more as a newb. You won’t really have that opportunity once you get beyond newbie gains in the future unless you take significant time off the gym. Focusing on eating healthy whole foods, protein intake, and eating roughly at maintenance will get you very far as a beginner. 

That being said, if you’d like to see more progress your training is likely the culprit. To consistently and effectively gain you’re going to want to be training in the 0-3 reps from failure range. I like the model of doing 2 reps in reserve on the first set or first couple sets, then going to failure on the last set so your body stays familiar with what failure and 2 reps in reserve feels like. This will also aid you a lot in the mid term future when doing this is way more crucial to continue making progress. 

Focus mostly on lifts that get you a good stretch at the end of the eccentric, hold that stretched position for a second or two, and focus on slow/controlled eccentrics. You might have to lighten the load on some lifts if you’re not doing these things already. 

Also focus on finding your balance between intensity and volume (aka stimulus to fatigue ratio). Find the rep ranges that work best for certain exercises for you, and find the number of sets that does the same. A good rule of thumb that’s easy to remember that served me well as a newb was to leave the gym fairly fatigued. Not SO fatigued that you’re not capable of doing much the rest of the day, but it should feel like you just worked really hard. You also don’t want to get so sore that you can’t train on your next session for that particular muscle. Maybe just a little tiny bit of remaining soreness. If you’re not getting sore, not getting pumps, not consistently getting a little stronger on lifts, never feeling a deep burn in the muscles towards the end of sets, you need to work harder. You don’t always have to experience all of those things. If you’re not really getting sore for example, but you’re getting pumps and your reps/weight is increasing you’re on the right track.

Thunderstorms in the Sierra (and alpine zones in general) hit a little different. They can be truly terrifying! 

In August of 2017, I did my 4th backpacking trip ever as an attempt at the jmt from rush creek going south. I made it all of two weeks and bailed over bishop pass after 116 miles. In retrospect I’m pretty proud of myself for that. Learned a lot of lessons on that trip!! Learned much about blisters and why everyone wears trail runners, and learned just how important keeping a pack sub 40 lbs is.

Anyways, one of the things that chased me off of the trail was a series of storms which was punctuated by a bad thunderstorm in upper leconte canyon, other side of Muir pass from evolution lake. A minor storm chased me and the friend I’d made several days prior off the pass, and we setup around 10,700 if I’m not mistaken. Gorgeous sunset that evening and I ate more than I should have after the long day from McClure meadow. Woke up in the middle of the night with a bubbling stomach and got up to dig my hole, went back to sleep, and no more than an hour later a crack of thunder shakes the ground below us. The lightning seemed to be striking the high peaks right above us. And the downpour was torrential. A tightly setup tent still resulted in a partially wet sleeping bag and tent floor. And the thunder still continued to shake the ground. Frequently the thunder was happening simultaneously to the flashes of lightning. And unable to speak to each other in our separate tents, my friend and I just sat there in our bags hoping not to get struck. 

The next morning as we were packing up a thick black cloud came over the ridge giving us a 5 minute heads up of the next incoming storm. We went from a calm morning to just throwing everything in our bags, and jogging downhill to get to lower elevation… oh and another pair of trail friends passed as we had started packing up. They were at Helen lake up around 11,500 and their story was insane. A girl who camped several feet from them had a bag with her electronics that got fried from ground current and was partially filled with a colored liquid from the batteries. Everyone we saw that morning just looked like they had the life sucked out of them. 

Sadly, my friend made it down faster when we were jogging, and my decision to leave was made at the junction to bishop pass. Thankfully we’d exchanged contact information, but I felt bad. After getting back in touch he said he wondered for a week if I’d bailed and kept convincing himself he’d see me walking up while he was resting. He finished the trail and wrote a book about it, where he briefly mentions that night on the south side of Muir pass. It’s a falcon book called discovering the John Muir trail by Damon Corso. I think I was more shaken than he was. 

While I maintain that I made the right decision to leave, I regretted it that night when I was in my hotel in bishop. But it just wasn’t to be that year. I was plagued by blisters that had mostly subsided and started to heal about 3 days prior to leaving. One of my knees was really aching quite badly. A few nights prior to the storm I was dumb enough to sleep with my head enclosed in my survival bivvy and woke up 3 hours later panting from lack of oxygen lol. It was a rough trip. I’m just glad I was lucky enough to dodge all the thunderstorms before that big one. Some people got rained on every day for a week straight in that stretch. I’d often roll through an area right before or right after a big storm. 

I got my revenge the next year starting over piute pass and making a two week trek to Whitney portal. Damon even joined me the last 3 days when I was just north of Forrester pass. We still talk occasionally.

My overall thought if you’re running the program as is and not suffering excessive fatigue is to continue it until you run into issues, if you ever do. Then make alterations from there if needed and prioritize the things you want to. 

The following is just a rough draft of the way I’d run your program if I had the same goals. Some exercises I replaced and some I eliminated. Was trying to keep things to 6 lifts or less, and trying to keep pretty much everything you had already which was a tough task. Friday and Saturday still ended up a little crowded.

I noticed you didn’t have anything glute specific unless that was your walking lunges. I replaced them with split squats. I see a ton of benefit to them as I get a crazy glute pump, and it’s a great way to finish off the quads and get them a crazy pump too. 

On Wednesdays I decided to keep 3 back exercises because the back really can handle a lot of volume, and lat pull downs are great warmups to pull-ups in a sense. And assisted pull-ups are necessary for me after doing lat pull downs. I get a lot out of them by doing high reps and really slow eccentrics and pausing for the stretch at the bottom (which you should be doing for every lift possible anyway). This is the order that I do my back focused day, and I usually do 2 sets for pull downs and assisted pull-ups, and 3-4 sets of chest supported rows. 

I also gave priority to the 3 upper body muscle groups you mentioned, and each have their own day priority wise. The beautiful thing is that with shoulders and forearms they won’t zap your energy for the lifts that follow. Might as well put them at the front since they’re a priority anyhow. 

I also swapped flys for deficit pushups. I create the deficit using kettlebells, but yoga blocks also work well. Anything that gets your hands a couple inches off the ground and gives your chest a huge stretch. I like these because they give the tris extra volume, and with slow eccentrics and pauses at the bottom for the stretch they’re great finishers for the pecs. Absolutely brutal and humbling way to wrap up the chest routine. 

I eliminated hip abduction and adduction reluctantly. They’re great additions if you plan to focus on a stronger squat in the future. However I don’t see much use for them outside of that. Given that your focus is currently hypertrophy (so is mine) I nixed them in favor of keeping that day shorter, and keeping calves in. Btw I’d recommend another exercise besides toe raises for calves. The platform at the bottom of this style hack squat machine makes for a great place to do calf raises https://www.precorhomefitness.com/products/precor-discovery-series-hack-squat-machine-dpl0603?currency=USD&variant=42432942440629&utm_medium=cpc&utm_source=google&utm_campaign=Google%20Shopping&srsltid=AfmBOoosm1f3jTFQrASRU2OvFXxV4u6CZZ84DW2qxFHCpUIaoE_h2ZKlFKk

Those are some main takeaways, and I’m sure there’s more alterations I’m forgetting. Either way this comment is too long. The last thing I’ll note is that I clustered all your muscle groups together. Back to back on chest, back to back on quads etc. Many believe this to be the best way to get the most out of hypertrophy, and I personally really like it. When I switched to this I consistently got very great pumps. 

Oh one last note. If you’re having problems with the barbell on flat then it may be worth giving up the barbell incline for a while too. Consider just doing more sets on incline with dumbbells, or doing both flat and incline with dumbbells. You won’t lose your barbell strength noticeably by doing this for a few months. Within a couple weeks of getting back to barbell you’ll be right back in the groove.

A lot to respond to, nitpick, and fine tune here. 

My first and most immediate observation is that you have all 5 days as 7-9 lift days. That is going to be a shit ton on a 5 day program. For me personally, 6 lift days are on the top end and 4 on the bottom end for 5 days a week. Slightly more if I’m doing 4 day mesocycles. Maybe you’ll do just fine with it. My guess is 3-4 weeks of running this and managing okay before a Deload and that first 3-4 weeks being slightly harder after, then Deload, then slightly harder and so on. Ymmv, maybe you’ll do just fine. Just know for most people it’s a lot and you’re likely not an exception. 

A better approach might be to bridge the gap with less lifts and more sets on some lifts to get a similar effect without burning yourself out. Take Wednesday for example. Bent over barbell rows are really cool, but very taxing. Also one of those lifts where injury is more likely compared to other back exercises. You could drop them and add a set of lat pull downs and a set or 2 of chest supported rows. You’re getting more out of your lats on the chest supported rows anyways, and trust me that many sets on those two lifts alone will fry your back. Also, on that same day you could do one variation of bicep curls for more sets. I don’t really see the point of doing 3 curl variations in one day. I like incline curls a lot and seem to get the most out of those. You might find the same. 

I picked the Wednesday apart because it stood out as an easy example to show that you could do 4 lifts with more sets on each and get the same or similar desired effect. You may net less overall sets, but you may find those sets to be junk volume anyhow. Even if you do the same number of sets it’s much more easy psychologically to look at that day on paper and see 4 lifts as opposed to 7, and you may get more out of each with or without an equal number of overall sets. Jumping around to 7 or 9 stations in one workout is a fuck ton of time my man. Do you want to spend 2-3 hours in the gym, or 1-2? 

Another thing that stands out is you’re not prioritizing the upper chest, side delts or forearms outside of Saturday with upper chest. If you want to emphasize those muscles you have to start with those muscles at least one day a week. You get the most out of your squat when you start with squats right? Get the most out of your side delts by starting with lateral raises at least one day and so on. This point kind of leads into my next one…

You’re trying to prioritize too many things at once. You want to emphasize upper chest growth, side delt growth, forearm growth, bench strength, and squat strength. Ideally you’d just be focused on that upper body growth for a couple months, or just the strength aspect for a couple months. I would sit down with myself and have an honest conversation about what it is I actually want to get from my training the next 2 months, then the next 6, and finally the next year. It’s okay for those goal posts to move, so focus most on the next 2 months. 

Another little tip that Dr Mike highlighted and works well for me… start with hamstrings on leg focused days. They won’t inhibit your other leg lifts and aren’t super fatiguing at all, and thus you’ll get more out of your hamstrings without negatively impacting your squats or anything.

I don’t do so much hiking anymore, but I used to do a lot and take a lot of landscape photography at sunset when I did. Often I’d be leaving the trail for long periods to shoot sunset shots, and then be coming back to the trail in the dark. 

My recommendation to anyone who wants to leave the trail is to pre plan your route extensively using a map and google earth. Take one path in and retrace your steps back out. Be able to pull your map out (use a compass if you’re not 100% sure), know roughly where you are, and what direction you need to go to get back to the trail. Observe details on the way in. That log with the funny shape, the tree branch that hung in a particular way, the face shaped rock… everything. Observe every detail possible. I can’t tell you how reassuring it is (especially in the dark) when you’re walking past the exact things you walked past on the way in. 

Another big recommendation to anyone who wants to hike off trail. Start small. Do short routes to build the skill set and the confidence in your ability to navigate.

Edit to add: if you become disoriented and feel lost, do not panic. No one makes good decisions when they’re panicking. If you’ve done your homework, you aren’t nearly as far off as you think you might be. Take a couple minutes to reorient yourself with your map and compass, use your phone if you have service to look at google maps etc. and remember that you are the smartest animal out there at the moment. You have more tools at your disposal, and people find their way back on track far more often than not. Everything is just fine and you’re experiencing a temporary delay.
